title: Lahore to Islamabad in an Atto 3 — one stop, 4h 55m door to door
content:
Did the M-2 run on Saturday and it is now genuinely a one-stop trip. Left Lahore at 92 percent, sat at 110 km/h with the AC on, and rolled into the Bhera service area with 34 percent left after 265 km.

Charged for 28 minutes to 78 percent, which was more than enough for the remaining 110 km plus city driving. Total door to door was 4 hours 55 minutes including the stop, so maybe 20 minutes more than I would have taken in a petrol car.

Two things worth knowing. Real-world consumption at motorway speed was 17.8 kWh/100km, noticeably worse than the 15.2 I see around town, so do not plan on the NEDC number. And the fast charger at Bhera tapers hard past 80 percent, so it is quicker to leave at 78 and stop again than to wait it out.

title: Six months and 11,000 km with a ZS EV — actual running costs
content:
I kept every charging receipt since January, so here are real numbers rather than estimates.

Of 11,000 km, roughly 70 percent was charged at home on a 7.4 kW wallbox and 30 percent on public DC. Home charging worked out to about 42 rupees per unit on the protected slab, public DC averaged 71. Blended cost came to 3.4 rupees per kilometre.

My old 1.6 Corolla was doing about 12 km per litre, so call it 22 rupees per kilometre. Over 11,000 km that is a saving of roughly 205,000 rupees in fuel alone.

The honest caveats: I have had one unplanned service visit for a coolant pump, load-shedding means I sometimes cannot charge overnight, and resale value on EVs here is still an unknown. But on running cost the case is not close.

title: Buying your first EV in Pakistan? Check the connector before anything else
content:
Seeing a lot of posts from people about to buy an imported EV without checking what they can actually plug into, so here is the short version.

CCS2 is the safe choice. Almost every new public DC charger going up in Lahore, Islamabad and Karachi is CCS2, and every locally sold BYD, MG and Proton uses it.

CHAdeMO is the risk. It is fine if you are buying an imported Leaf and you live near DHA in Karachi, but there is essentially one reliable public CHAdeMO in the entire city. Anywhere else and you are on home AC charging only.

GB/T shows up on some directly imported Chinese cars. Public GB/T is close to non-existent here, so treat those as home-charge-only vehicles.

Type 2 is the AC standard and every modern EV has it. Slow, but universal — useful as a fallback everywhere.

Before you commit to a car, open the map, filter by its connector, and look at what is within 20 km of your home and office. If the answer is one station, think carefully.

title: Best fast charger in Karachi right now?
content:
Moved to DHA last month and still working out where to charge reliably. So far DHA Charging Hub has been the only one I trust — six ports, never queued, and the CHAdeMO actually works, which matters because my Leaf cannot use anything else.

Clifton Fast Charge is closer to my office but one of its two ports has been dead for weeks and 50 kW is slow for a 62 kWh pack.

Anyone found something better on the far side of the city? Ideally somewhere near Korangi or SITE. Happy to pay more per unit for something that is actually working when I arrive.

title: MG ZS EV vs BYD Atto 3 — Which should I buy?
content:
I own the ZS EV and my brother is about to buy his first EV, so I have spent a lot of time comparing these two lately. Here is my honest take having driven both.

The Atto 3 wins on battery. 60.5 kWh against the ZS EV 50.3 kWh is a real difference on intercity runs — roughly one fewer stop between Lahore and Islamabad. Build quality inside is also a step up.

The ZS EV wins on price and on service network. MG has more workshops in more cities, and when something needs fixing that matters more than people expect.

Charging speed is closer than the spec sheets suggest. The Atto 3 peaks higher but both taper hard past 60 percent on the chargers we actually have here.

If you drive mostly in-city and want the lower price, ZS EV. If you regularly do long runs, Atto 3.

title: New EV policy announced by Government
content:
The updated policy landed this week and there are a few things worth reading carefully rather than from the headlines.

Duty relief on imported EVs has been extended, which should hold prices roughly where they are rather than pushing them down much further.

More interesting is the charging infrastructure clause — new commercial buildings above a certain size will need to provision for EV charging at the design stage. That is the sort of thing that takes three years to show up but changes the map permanently.

What is still missing is anything meaningful on grid capacity. Every operator I have spoken to says the transformer, not the charger, is the bottleneck.

title: My first month with BYD Atto 3
content:
Thirty days and about 1,400 km in. Short version: I would buy it again, with two caveats.

What works. The ride is genuinely comfortable on bad roads, which matters more here than any performance figure. Charging at home overnight has completely removed the fuel-station routine from my week. Consumption has settled at 16.2 kWh/100km in mixed driving.

What does not. The infotainment rotates the screen as a party trick and is slower than it should be. And the regenerative braking has two settings, neither of which is proper one-pedal driving.

The caveats: you need home charging for this to make sense, and you need to accept that long trips still require planning.

title: Home charger installation — what it actually costs
content:
Just had a 7.4 kW wallbox installed in Lahore and there is very little honest information about pricing, so here are my real numbers.

Charger unit: 148,000. Installation labour: 22,000. Dedicated 40A breaker and cabling for an 18 metre run: 31,000. Earthing rod, because the existing one was not adequate: 9,000.

Total: 210,000 rupees.

The thing nobody warned me about is the earthing. Two of the three installers I got quotes from did not even mention it. Ask about it explicitly — a wallbox on poor earthing is a genuine safety problem, not a technicality.

title: Karachi to Hyderabad and back on one charge
content:
Did the round trip on Sunday — 162 km each way on the M-9, so 324 km total — without stopping to charge. Left at 96 percent, got home on 19 percent.

The motorway is flat and the surface is good, so consumption was better than I expected at 17.1 kWh/100km sitting at 110 km/h with the AC running properly.

If you have a smaller pack this is comfortably a one-stop trip. There is nothing usable in Hyderabad itself yet, so plan on charging before you leave Karachi either way.

title: Charging etiquette — we need to talk about it
content:
Three times this month I have arrived at a charger to find a car sitting at 100 percent with the owner nowhere nearby. Once for over an hour.

We are a small enough community that this is still fixable by norms rather than rules. A few suggestions.

Move your car when it is done, or at least be reachable. Do not use a 150 kW bay for a top-up you could do on AC. If someone is waiting and you are past 80 percent, the taper means you are giving up very little by unplugging.

None of this is difficult and it stops being a problem entirely if we all just do it.

title: Winter range loss — what to expect in northern Pakistan
content:
With Murree and Naran trips coming up for a lot of people, worth setting expectations on cold weather.

In Islamabad at around 5 degrees I lose roughly 15 percent against my summer average. Above Murree, closer to freezing, it has been nearer 25 percent — and that is before the climbing, which costs more again.

The practical advice: precondition the cabin while still plugged in, use seat heating rather than blasting the cabin heater, and treat the trip computer as optimistic until you are back below the snow line.

title: First public charger in Faisalabad is live
content:
It finally happened. A 60 kW CCS2 unit went live near the Kohinoor area this week — as far as I know the first public DC charger in Faisalabad.

Tried it yesterday. Pulled 54 kW steady, card payment worked, and the site is lit and staffed in the evening. Tariff is 72 per unit, which is in line with Lahore.

Small thing nationally, big thing here. Up to now the honest answer to anyone in Faisalabad asking about an EV was that they needed home charging and no intercity plans.
